strengths: Compelling and timely core thesis: shifting the burden of repository-level software engineering from fragile and expensive test-time agentic scaffolding into model weights via scalable, verified mid-training.

Rigorously designed data construction and validation pipeline: converting noisy diffs into deterministic, minimal Search/Replace blocks verified through round-trip re-application, and linking PRs with original issue discussions to provide authentic user intent.

Comprehensive and fair experimental comparisons: the paper controls for compute and token budget against a carefully reproduced StarCoder2-style mid-training baseline (17.7B vs 17.4B tokens) and demonstrates substantial gains (+8.6% on Lite, +10.2% on Verified) over that baseline.

Strong empirical performance: Clean-PR (32B) outperforms 72B models (Lingma-SWE, SWE-Fixer) and prior 32B agentic systems (SWE-Gym) on SWE-bench Lite and Verified using a lightweight Agentless workflow.

Thorough ablations and generalization checks: the study effectively isolates the gains from the Search/Replace format, issue context augmentation, and error-driven SFT data; it also evaluates HumanEval and LiveCodeBench, showing that Clean-PR avoids catastrophic forgetting.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to Python: despite curating a 12-language corpus and showing that multilingual mid-training benefits Python SWE-bench, the paper does not evaluate downstream repo-level editing performance on multilingual benchmarks (such as Multi-SWE-bench or SWE-PolyBench, both cited in the text).

Single model architecture: all mid-training experiments are conducted exclusively on Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Base. While the computational expenditure is understandable, empirical validation on an alternative architecture (e.g., DeepSeek-Coder or Llama) would confirm that the data pipeline transfers across different model families.

Minor consistency discrepancy: in Section 3.2 (Paragraph 2), the text states that 'The Base + SFT model... achieves only 10.3% on Lite', whereas Table 6 reports 11.3% for the corresponding row (Qwen-Coder-32B-Base, Mid-Train Setting: None, SFT: ✓).

strengths: Sound and scalable data construction pipeline: The paper identifies key failure modes of raw PR ingestion (bot activity, formatting churn, lack of user intent) and addresses them systematically through issue linking, deterministic Search/Replace conversion, and round-trip verification (Algorithm 1).

Strong empirical gains with low inference overhead: Mid-training Qwen2.5-Coder-32B on Clean-PR yields substantial improvements on SWE-bench Lite (+13.6% absolute over instruct) and Verified (+12.3%), outperforming larger 72B baselines and agentic systems (e.g., SWE-Gym 32B) under a simple, linear Agentless protocol.

Comprehensive and informative ablations: The experimental section effectively isolates the impact of the verified Search/Replace format vs. unified diffs, issue augmentation vs. PR descriptions alone, and error-driven negative augmentation in SFT.

Mitigation of catastrophic forgetting: The analysis in Section 3.3 and Figure 2 shows that training on verified context-matching blocks actually improves general coding benchmarks (HumanEval and LiveCodeBench), unlike standard diff pretraining which caused degradation.

Rigorous data decontamination: The authors implement multi-layered decontamination combining repository-level blocklists, exact SHA-256 file matching, and n-gram / Jaccard similarity filtering against SWE-bench evaluation instances.
weaknesses: Lack of evaluation on multilingual SWE benchmarks: While the Clean-PR corpus spans 12 programming languages and the paper claims benefits from multi-language mid-training, the downstream evaluation is restricted to Python benchmarks (SWE-bench Lite and Verified). Evaluating on Multi-SWE-bench or SWE-PolyBench would significantly strengthen the claims regarding multilingual repo-level capabilities.

Single model family evaluation: The entire mid-training recipe is demonstrated exclusively on Qwen2.5-Coder-32B. Although compute constraints (over 10 days on 32x H200) are acknowledged, experiments on smaller models (e.g., 7B or 14B) or an alternative model family would establish whether the findings generalize across architectures.

Composition of the SFT data: The stepwise SFT relies on trajectories mined from SWE-rebench, SWE-Gym, and SWE-bench-Live. While test instances are decontaminated, this SFT distribution is closely aligned with the SWE-bench evaluation format, making it harder to distinguish the exact boundary between mid-training representation learning and task-specific SFT alignment.

Pass@k potential remains unrealized: Figure 3 demonstrates strong potential from test-time sampling (up to 41.5% Pass@10 on Verified), but the paper does not explore even simple execution-based filtering or lightweight rerankers to test whether these candidate gains can be converted into single-run improvements.

strengths: High-impact data engineering and curation contribution: The paper addresses the crucial 'noise-validity gap' in GitHub PRs by constructing a massive, verified corpus of 2M PRs (17.7B tokens) across 12 languages with deterministic round-trip verification of minimal unique Search/Replace blocks.

Strong and convincing empirical gains: Mid-training with Clean-PR combined with error-augmented SFT yields significant improvements on SWE-bench Lite (24.3%) and Verified (30.6%), surpassing prior 32B systems (e.g., SWE-Gym at 20.6%) and matching or exceeding 72B systems under a simplified Agentless inference protocol.

Thorough and principled ablations: The evaluation carefully isolates each key design choice—contrasting Search/Replace with unified diffs, quantifying the value of linked issue context over raw PR descriptions, and demonstrating the effectiveness of error-driven distractor augmentation during SFT.

Insightful analysis of catastrophic forgetting: The paper shows that mid-training on verified Search/Replace blocks preserves and even enhances general coding benchmarks (HumanEval and LiveCodeBench), in stark contrast to unified diff pretraining which degrades general reasoning.

Rigorous decontamination pipeline: The authors implement a multi-layered decontamination strategy encompassing repository exclusion, exact SHA-256 matching, and n-gram / Jaccard overlap filtering against SWE-bench test sets.
weaknesses: Lack of multilingual downstream evaluation: Although Clean-PR is constructed and trained across 12 languages (with 'All Languages' showing gains over 'Python Only'), the downstream evaluation is restricted to Python-only SWE-bench benchmarks. Evaluating on multilingual benchmarks cited in the paper (e.g., Multi-SWE-bench or SWE-PolyBench) would directly validate whether non-Python editing capabilities actually transfer.

Exploration limited to a single model architecture/scale: Due to heavy compute requirements (259 wall-clock hours on 32 H200 GPUs), experiments are conducted solely on Qwen2.5-Coder-32B. Including smaller-scale checkpoints (e.g., 7B or 14B) would strengthen claims regarding the generalizability of the mid-training recipe across scales.

Sensitivity to intermediate error-mining model: The error-driven augmentation pipeline relies on erroneous trajectories mined from Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct. The paper does not analyze the sensitivity of the final SFT stage to the choice or strength of this noise-generating model.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental challenge in repository-level code editing by internalizing multi-file editing capabilities into model weights, reducing reliance on heavy test-time agent scaffolding.

Proposes a well-engineered and rigorous data construction pipeline, including round-trip verification to derive deterministic, minimal Search/Replace blocks from noisy PR diffs, and issue linking to ground edits in user problem statements.

Comprehensive experimental validation on SWE-bench Lite and Verified, where the proposed Clean-PR mid-training with Agentless SFT yields strong gains (e.g., reaching 24.3% on Lite and 30.6% on Verified for Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, surpassing 72B baselines under a simplified Agentless protocol).

Extensive ablation studies and validation checks, including format ablations (Search/Replace vs. Unified Diff), issue description grounding, error-driven augmentation, catastrophic forgetting analysis on HumanEval/LiveCodeBench, scale generalization (7B), multilingual generalization, and transfer to agentic workflows (OpenHands).

Exemplary decontamination and leakage analysis, employing multi-level lexical filtering (exact file hashes, 15-gram matches) alongside semantic similarity quintile correlation to verify that gains are driven by generalisation rather than benchmark contamination.
weaknesses: The scope constraint restricting training instances to PRs modifying at most five core files biases the training distribution toward local or modular edits, leaving broad architectural changes spanning dozens of files under-addressed.

The computational investment required for full mid-training (259 wall-clock hours on 32 H200 GPUs) is substantial, making complete pre-training reproduction difficult for resource-constrained academic groups, although the planned release of the curated dataset partially mitigates this concern.

While transfer to OpenHands is demonstrated, the primary evaluation remains centered around SWE-bench benchmarks; evaluating performance on real-world iterative human-in-the-loop developer workflows would provide further insight into practical usability.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental challenge in repository-level software engineering by investigating how much editing capability can be internalised into model weights via mid-training, reducing reliance on complex agentic test-time scaffolding.

Comprehensive and rigorous data engineering pipeline (Clean-PR) that transforms raw, noisy GitHub PRs into verified Search/Replace blocks with deterministic round-trip verification, coupled with issue-intent augmentation and thorough noise filtering.

Convincing empirical performance: fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Coder-32B achieves 24.3% on SWE-bench Lite and 30.6% on SWE-bench Verified under a lightweight Agentless workflow, outperforming substantially larger 72B models and agentic baselines.

Extensive ablation studies and validations: the paper systematically isolates the impact of the Search/Replace representation, issue linking, error-driven negative augmentation, multi-language data scaling, and model size (7B vs. 32B), while also testing agentic transfer (OpenHands) and monitoring catastrophic forgetting on HumanEval and LiveCodeBench.

Careful decontamination protocol combining repository-level blocklisting, exact file hashing, n-gram overlap, and a semantic leakage analysis demonstrating that test instances with high similarity to training data do not exhibit higher resolve rates.
weaknesses: The Agentless-aligned SFT stage relies on trajectories derived from existing SWE benchmark collections (SWE-rebench, SWE-Gym, and SWE-bench-Live); although evaluation repos are strictly held out, it remains reliant on benchmark-style curated trajectory data for downstream alignment.

Computational requirements for full multi-language mid-training (259 wall-clock hours on 32 H200 GPUs) are high, which may hinder easy reproduction for academic labs with modest resources, though the authors partially mitigate this by providing a Python-only setting.

strengths: Substantial and convincing empirical results on SWE-bench Lite (24.3%) and Verified (30.6%) using Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, outperforming competitive agent-based frameworks and matching or exceeding 72B baselines under a deterministic Agentless protocol.

A well-engineered data construction and verification pipeline: transforming raw, noisy PR diffs into minimal unique Search/Replace edit blocks with deterministic round-trip verification, while augmenting PR context with linked issue discussions.

Comprehensive and rigorous ablation studies that effectively disentangle the contributions of Search/Replace vs. Unified Diff, linked issues vs. PR descriptions, mid-training vs. SFT-only, and error-driven negative augmentation.

Extensive evaluation across diverse dimensions: demonstrating scalability to 7B models, transfer to multi-turn agentic settings (OpenHands CodeActAgent), cross-lingual generalization on Multi-SWE-bench Flash, and verification that general coding capability is preserved without catastrophic forgetting (evaluating HumanEval and LiveCodeBench).
Thorough decontamination protocol combining repository-level blacklisting, SHA-256 hash checks, n-gram/Jaccard overlap filtering, and embedding-based semantic similarity quintile analysis.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is primarily centered on data engineering and pipeline alignment: the training protocol decomposes tasks along established Agentless workflows, and mid-training on version control data is conceptually well-known, even though the specific execution and verification here are superior.

The final downstream performance relies substantially on the second-stage stepwise SFT constructed from existing curated benchmarks (SWE-rebench, SWE-Gym, SWE-bench-Live); while SWE-bench test repos are excluded, the relative contribution between the massive 17.7B PR mid-training and this specialized SFT stage could be more sharply delineated.

The data selection heuristic restricts PRs to those modifying at most five core files and truncates context via 100k-token windowing, which naturally biases the model toward localized edits and limits evaluation on cross-cutting architectural modifications.

High computational requirement for end-to-end replication (requiring 259 wall-clock hours across 32 NVIDIA H200 GPUs for mid-training), which restricts easy reproducibility for academic research groups lacking frontier-scale compute infrastructure.
